title: When Two Sources Disagree, Nothing Automated Notices
description: An AI coding pipeline picks one clinical source and codes from it — it doesn't compare that source against a contradicting one elsewhere in the same chart, which is exactly the pattern a human reviewer has to catch.

learningObjectives.text: Recognize that automated coding pipelines select a single source rather than reconciling conflicting sources
Identify the correct compliant response to contradictory clinical documentation

contentSections.body: An AI clinical coding system reviews a discharge summary where the attending's final note reads 'pneumonia, resolved,' but a nursing note from the same day documents the patient still on IV antibiotics with audible crackles on exam. The system codes from the attending's note — typically the higher-authority source — and finalizes the encounter as resolved pneumonia, no complication. It never flags that the two notes contradict each other, because nothing in its pipeline is built to compare sources against each other for consistency. It's built to pick the most likely single source and map it to a code.

Automated coding systems are optimized to produce one confident answer per document. Detecting that two legitimate sources in the same chart disagree is a different task entirely — cross-document comparison, not per-document extraction — and most pipelines were never built to do it.

In compliant clinical documentation improvement (CDI) practice, contradictory documentation like this is resolved with a **physician query**: a formal, compliant request asking the attending to clarify or confirm the discrepancy, before a final code is assigned. Silently picking one source over the other — whichever the model weighted more heavily, or whichever a reviewer personally finds more credible — isn't just a coding-accuracy risk, it's a compliance gap. Query practice exists precisely for this situation: real disagreement between legitimate documentation sources that only the treating clinician can actually resolve.

contentSections.code:
Attending discharge note: "Pneumonia, resolved."
Nursing note, same date: "Patient remains on IV antibiotics, crackles present on auscultation."
AI-assigned code: pneumonia, resolved, no complication — coded directly from the attending's note.
contentSections.question: What's the correct next step when a reviewer notices this contradiction?

options.label: Issue a compliant physician query to resolve the contradiction before finalizing the code
Accept the AI-assigned code — the attending's note is the higher-authority source
Silently override the code to match the nursing note instead

feedback.issue-compliant-query: Correct. Neither source should be silently preferred over the other — that's a judgment call only the treating clinician can actually resolve. A compliant physician query asks the attending to clarify or confirm which documentation reflects the patient's actual status, and the final code should reflect that clarified answer, not a guess about which note to trust.
feedback.accept-ai-code: Authority of a note type doesn't resolve a genuine clinical contradiction — an attending's summary note written at discharge can be inaccurate or outdated relative to same-day clinical findings documented elsewhere. Coding from the higher-authority source without resolving the conflict risks finalizing an inaccurate code.
feedback.override-to-nursing-note: Silently picking the other source has the same underlying problem as accepting the AI's pick — it's a reviewer substituting their own guess for a clarification only the attending can actually provide. Compliant practice resolves genuine documentation conflicts through a query, not through picking a side.

contentSections.flawExplanation: Both notes are legitimate, contemporaneous, signed documentation — neither is inherently more trustworthy just because of who wrote it or when. An AI pipeline built to extract one confident answer per document has no mechanism to notice that a second, equally valid document in the same chart says something different. Only a human (or a query back to the human who can actually resolve it) can catch that kind of cross-document conflict.

contentSections.body: The edge case that matters isn't a single wrong field — it's when two legitimate sources in the same chart disagree and nothing in the pipeline is built to notice. Recognizing that pattern and escalating it through a compliant query, rather than silently picking a side, is the actual skill this module trains.

title: Two Things Being Mentioned Together Isn't the Same as One Causing the Other
description: AI coding pipelines are pattern-matchers — they notice when two conditions appear near each other in a note, but coding a causal relationship between them requires documentation that actually states the causation, not just co-occurrence.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish co-occurrence of two documented findings from a documented causal relationship between them
Identify when a code requiring causation is assigned from documentation that only supports co-occurrence

contentSections.body: A trauma note documents a patient with pneumonia and, separately, a recent choking episode. Imaging shows a lobar infiltrate consistent with bacterial pneumonia; the aspirate culture came back negative. An AI coding pipeline sees both "pneumonia" and "aspiration event" documented in the same chart and assigns J69.0, aspiration pneumonia — a code that specifically requires a *causal* link between the aspiration and the pneumonia. Nothing in the note actually says the aspiration caused this pneumonia. The two things happened to the same patient; the pipeline coded them as if one caused the other.

This is a distinct edge case from the previous lesson's source-contradiction pattern — here there's no disagreement between sources, just a pipeline that treats **co-occurrence as causation**. Some ICD-10 codes (aspiration pneumonia is a textbook example) specifically require documentation that one condition caused or is linked to the other, not just that both are present in the same encounter. A model trained to notice related terms appearing near each other has no reliable way to distinguish "the note says A caused B" from "the note happens to mention A and B" — that distinction lives entirely in how the documentation is phrased, which requires reading for causal language, not just detecting relevant terms.

The review skill here is checking, specifically for any code whose definition includes a causal or linking requirement, whether the documentation actually states that link — or whether it's being inferred from two findings simply appearing in the same chart.

contentSections.scenario:
Trauma note documents: pneumonia (imaging shows lobar infiltrate consistent with bacterial pneumonia) and, separately, a choking/aspiration event. Aspirate culture is negative. No sentence in the note states the aspiration caused or is linked to the pneumonia.

AI-assigned code: J69.0 (Aspiration pneumonia).
contentSections.question: What's the actual problem with assigning J69.0 here?

options.label: J69.0 specifically requires documentation that the aspiration caused the pneumonia — co-occurrence of both findings in the same chart isn't the same as a documented causal link
The code is wrong because it doesn't specify the severity of the pneumonia
The negative aspirate culture is irrelevant to whether J69.0 is the correct code

feedback.requires-documented-causation: Correct. Aspiration pneumonia as a diagnosis requires the documentation to actually establish that the aspiration caused this pneumonia episode — not just that both findings exist somewhere in the chart. Imaging consistent with ordinary bacterial pneumonia, without a stated causal link, doesn't meet that bar. The right next step is a provider query asking whether a causal link is actually intended, not assigning the code from co-occurrence alone.
feedback.wrong-pneumonia-severity: Severity specification isn't the issue being raised here — the deeper problem is that the code category itself (aspiration pneumonia, which requires documented causation) may not even apply given what the documentation actually supports.
feedback.culture-result-irrelevant: The culture result is a real clinical detail worth noting, but it isn't what actually settles the coding question here — only whether the documentation states a causal link does. A negative culture doesn't rule out aspiration pneumonia (it's often culture-negative, especially early or when chemical rather than infectious), and a positive one wouldn't establish causation on its own either. Either way, the correct next step is the same: a provider query, not a coder's own clinical inference from lab results.

contentSections.mechanism: Pattern-matching systems reliably detect that two clinical terms appear in the same document. They do not reliably distinguish documentation that establishes a causal or linking relationship between those terms from documentation that simply mentions both — that distinction requires reading the actual language connecting (or not connecting) the two findings, which is exactly the judgment layer a human reviewer provides for any code whose definition depends on a documented causal link.

contentSections.body: Whenever a code's definition requires one condition to be linked to or caused by another — not just present alongside it — check that the documentation actually states that link. An AI pipeline that notices both terms in the same chart has no way to tell you whether the documentation supports causation or just co-occurrence; that's a reading task, not a detection task.
